subtype: Approach: revising the routine when it feels forced [Revision]
passage: Francis, you look tired of your nightly calls, so let me, Ujjwal, tell you about mine. My wife and I were apart for two years when I worked on a ship. In the beginning we called every night, no matter what. By the ninth month we were both doing it like homework. "How was your day?" "Fine. And yours?" Ten minutes of nothing, then sleep. One evening she said, "Do we even enjoy this?" We laughed, because it was true. We changed the rule. Short messages every day: a photo of tea, a line from a song. Two real calls each week, with no phone in the other hand. The relationship felt light again, and calls became something to look forward to.

qa.q: How many real calls each week did Ujjwal and Ujjwal's wife keep?
qa.a: They kept two real calls each week.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling by the ninth month of nightly calls?
qa.a: Ujjwal was bored and dutiful, treating the calls like homework rather than a joy.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: They admitted together that the calls felt like a chore and changed the rule, because honesty allowed a lighter routine that they actually wanted.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's wife have felt when she asked if they even enjoyed it?
qa.a: She was probably tired of the routine too but worried about saying it, and the shared laugh shows relief at finding both felt the same.

grounding: Shows a couple revising a call routine that had become a chore, switching to short daily messages and two proper calls each week.
